alt: Three cards show the functions in the specification: serving the economy, facilitating social mobility and fostering social cohesion. Below, functionalists say education serves society as a whole, Marxists say it serves capitalism, and feminists say it has reproduced gender inequality.
caption: The specification lists three functions; the perspectives disagree about whom they really serve.

alt: A bridge labelled school joins the family on one side to wider society on the other. In the family children are judged by particularistic standards; in society everyone is judged by universalistic standards. School is meritocratic, builds a value consensus and selects people for future roles.
caption: School moves children from particularistic family rules to the universalistic rules of society.

after: ## 3.4.2 The relationship between education and capitalism
alt: Four matched pairs link school to work: obeying teachers and obeying managers; working for grades and working for wages; separate lessons and narrow tasks; competing for rank and competing for promotion. The result is a docile, obedient workforce too divided to challenge management. Below, alternative views from Willis, functionalists, feminists and interactionists.
caption: Social relationships at school mirror those at work, so school reproduces labour power.

alt: Bar chart: compared with a working-class boy, a service-class boy was four times as likely to be at school at 16, eight times at 17, ten times at 18 and eleven times as likely to attend university. Below, the three classes by father’s occupation and the all-male sample of over 8,000.
caption: The longer education goes on, the wider the class gap becomes.

alt: Three columns of explanations. Class: material deprivation, cultural deprivation and cultural capital. Gender: girls now outperform boys because of feminism, equal opportunities policies and fewer manual jobs for boys, though subject choice stays gendered. Ethnicity: material factors, language, an ethnocentric curriculum and institutional racism.
caption: Class, gender and ethnicity each have their own explanations, and they overlap.

alt: Parental choice and league tables make schools compete. Schools reintroduce streaming and setting and focus on the more able, while middle-class parents are better placed to use choice, so the market can widen class inequality.
caption: Competition between schools can help the middle class more than the working class.

alt: Three panels follow one highlighted pupil across maths, English and science. With streaming the pupil is in the lower group for every subject. With setting the pupil is in the top set for maths and science but a lower set for English. With mixed ability everyone is taught together.
caption: Streaming fixes one group for all subjects; setting can differ subject by subject.

alt: Two step-by-step columns. Ball at Beachside: middle-class pupils were more often placed in band 1 with higher teacher expectations, while band 2 was steered to easier exams and developed anti-school attitudes. Willis: twelve working-class lads formed a counter school culture, rejected school, and this suited them to manual work.
caption: Ball shows labelling through banding; Willis shows resistance that still led to manual work.
